qa_multi_document_information_integratio.question: How do different language model architectures, such as encoder-decoder models and masked language models, handle long input contexts or long text generation, and what are their respective challenges?
qa_multi_document_information_integratio.answer: Encoder-decoder models like Flan-UL2 are relatively robust to changes in relevant information position within their training-time sequence length, showing only a 1.9% absolute difference between best- and worst-case performance. However, decoder-only models like GPT-3.5-Turbo can experience significant performance degradation (over 20%) when relevant information is in the middle of long contexts. Masked language models (MLMs) like RoBERTa, when adapted for open-ended long text generation, face a 'collapse problem' where they generate uninformative and repetitive content for texts around 140 tokens, requiring specific techniques like Dynamic Sliding Window Attention (DSWA) and Linear Temperature Decay (LTD) to alleviate long-distance collapse and improve sampling.

ref.paper_title: Open-ended Long Text Generation via Masked Language Modeling
ref.content: Our preliminary study shows that pre-trained MLMs can merely generate short text and will collapse for long text modeling. To enhance the long text generation capability of MLMs, we introduce two simple yet effective strategies for the iterative NAR model: dynamic sliding window attention (DSWA) and linear temperature decay (LTD). It can alleviate long-distance collapse problems and achieve longer text generation with a flexible trade-off between performance and inference speedup.

ref.content: Through experiments, we found that: (1) pre-trained MLMs can achieve competitive performance in the iterative NAR fashion for open-ended short text generation (e.g., a paragraph with around 40 tokens), (2) pre-trained MLMs fail to model Open-LTG (with about 140 tokens on average), which will generate uninformative content with high-frequency and repeated tokens (e.g., “,” and “.”).

Flan-T5-XXL shows a similar trend, where longer input contexts result in a greater performance degradation when placing relevant information in the middle of the input context.

qa_multi_document_information_integratio.answer: For evaluating long text generation, metrics include BLEU, ROUGE, Lexical Repetition (LR), Semantic Repetition (SR), Distinct (D-n), BERTScore, Perplexity (PPL), METEOR, and human evaluations for Fluency, Coherence, and Relevance. qa_multi_document_information_integratio.question: Do language models exhibit positional biases when processing long input sequences, and how do these biases manifest?
qa_multi_document_information_integratio.answer: Yes, language models exhibit positional biases, often manifesting as a U-shaped performance curve where performance is lowest when relevant information is in the middle of long input contexts, and better when it's at the beginning (primacy bias) or end (recency bias). This U-shaped curve is observed in larger models (e.g., Llama-2 13B and 70B), while smaller models (e.g., Llama-2 7B) tend to be solely recency-biased. Instruction fine-tuning can slightly mitigate this bias, reducing worst-case performance disparity.

Furthermore, we observe a distinctive U-shaped performance curve (Figure 1); language model performance is highest when relevant information occurs at the very beginning (primacy bias) or end of its input context (recency bias), and performance significantly degrades when models must access and use information in the middle of their input context (§2.3).

qa_multi_document_information_integratio.question: What techniques are proposed to improve how language models handle or generate long texts and contexts?
qa_multi_document_information_integratio.answer: To improve long text generation, techniques like Dynamic Sliding Window Attention (DSWA) are used to alleviate long-distance collapse by restricting attention to neighbor tokens, and Linear Temperature Decay (LTD) is applied to improve sampling effectiveness by adjusting confidence scores during iterative refinement. For improving context utilization in long inputs, query-aware contextualization can dramatically improve performance on retrieval tasks, and instruction fine-tuning can help mitigate positional biases, although it minimally affects multi-document QA trends.

ref.content: With this strategy, we can alleviate the multi-modality problem by restricting the model to attend to the tokens in the window instead of the whole sequence, thus degenerating the multi-modal distribution into a uni-modal distribution.

ref.paper_title: Open-ended Long Text Generation via Masked Language Modeling
ref.content:
To further improve the effectiveness of sampling, we use the confidence-based iterative refinement by adjusting the temperature with linear schedule:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{P}(y_i | \mathcal{X}, \text{Win}(\mathcal{Y}_M)) &= \frac{\exp(u_i/T)}{\sum_{i'} \exp(u_{i'}/T)}, \\ T &= \beta * (1 - \frac{t}{T}), \end{aligned} \quad (8)$$
where  $\beta$  is hyper-parameter,  $t \in \{0, \dots, T\}$  is the current iteration step, and  $T$  is the maximum iteration step. Actually, the output distributions will be flattened when  $T > 1$ , and become sharp when  $T < 1$ . Therefore, by applying this strategy, we can penalize the distribution from peaked to flat in the former iteration steps and encourage it from flat to peaked in the later steps.

This discrepancy makes the model only refine a fraction of the low confidence tokens, which causes the degeneration in practice. Thus, we update all target tokens according to model predictions at each iteration step by utilizing the SMART mechanism (Ghazvininejad et al., 2020).
